title: What small tools do you build around your AI game dev workflow, and what happens when they break?
author: Embarrassed_Sort8987
selftext:
I’m a developer researching how people keep the small tools they build for their own workflow (scripts, asset pipelines, little helpers). In AI game dev, models and APIs change all the time, so I’m curious how that plays out for you.

The last time one of your tools stopped working because an API or a model changed, what did you do, and how long did it take to fix? Or did you just drop it?

I’m not selling or promoting anything, and I’ll share a summary of what I learn here.

replies.author: HunterIV4
replies.body:
>Do you have a rule of thumb for building tools that keep working for years?

"Vibe coding" that is actually functional has only really existed for about a year, *maybe* two. Probably not going to find much long-term data on this.

I personally ensure the AI is following my own coding practices and "human readable" with extensive documentation is standard. That way if I'm ever messing with the code base without access to models (usually from using up all my tokens) I can still keep working manually.

If I had some throwaway project that was totally vibe-coded and I didn't pay much attention to (I have a couple of these, mostly minor utility tools) and every frontier AI I'm subscribed to shut down tomorrow, I'd just swap to Qwen locally. It would be slower and need more manual work but as long as your harness doesn't suck and you keep the AI carefully scoped it's fine.

I use frontier models because they are faster and get more done in each step, not because I have to.

replies.author: Embarrassed_Sort8987
replies.body: Thanks, that’s really helpful. Do any of those throwaway tools ever end up being something you keep long term, or that someone else starts using?

replies.author: HunterIV4
replies.body:
Sure, I keep most of them. They're usually things that automate small parts of my job but aren't critical or help out someone with a tedious task they could do manually. For example, I have a script that automatically enters my timecard time on a rather annoying web interface, and an app I made for HR that automates new account creation in a way that's easier to validate and create than them manually entering everything into Excel. They work and aren't critical to operations so I've seen no reason to update them.

Likewise, in my current game I had the AI create a "fight club" that pulls from the game data and lets me test various combat encounters in a sandbox environment, complete with simulations of various conditions and JSON outputs I can use to graph or otherwise analyze parameters later. None of this code is going into the final game, but it helps me balance new content and get sanity checks on possible exploits or overly optimized loadouts. Same with a long-term sim; the game design allows for pseudo-offline progression (based on system clock), so I had the AI write a simulator for progression at various game states to get an idea of the resource and progression curves it creates so I can adjust it.

There's more, but those are the examples that come to mind. I'm sure there are things I could be doing that I'm not yet too.

replies.author: HunterIV4
replies.body:
>why would continuing development cause a tool to stop working?

I'll address this in a second.

>it feels like i'm legitimately having a discussion with people from mars. you guys' lines of logic don't even get into the same building as a real world software development process.

Maybe instead of being rude, you could actually take a few seconds to think about this. Like, *really* think about the context.

Let's imagine I build a tool with Claude. I don't know how the tool works, Claude does, but it works. It's version 1.0.

Five years from now, I want to add a few features, making it version 1.1. But somehow the anti-AI lobby has banned AI data centers and all the major AI players are shut down. So, if I want to **continue development**, I can't just ask Claude, can I? Claude is shut down.

If that update is critical, say things it was dependent on were updated and it no longer works, I need a way to update it.

Now, if you're already a software developer, the answer is obvious: write it yourself. I *am* a software developer, and have been coding since the 90s, so this is not particularly hard for me. That's why I wrote that I make sure it follows my coding practices and has documentation so *if* I need to manually update it I don't have to spend days figuring out WTF Claude did. I *can* do that, but it's annoying and tedious and the AI can do it with little extra time.

If you are *not* a software developer, and just vibe coded, this is a serious problem. Something like Qwen, which is a local model, would likely be sufficient for updates, depending on scope (and hardware access).

Maybe, rather than assuming everyone is talking about code that mysteriously stops working over time or that I said something like "the tool stops functioning if you can't continue developing it" more than the obvious "how do I continue development if my AI tools aren't available?", you can read the context and think about what's being said.

comments.author: playtetramental
comments.body:
My tools mostly break when I change the game. 

Tools for different versions of the game: When I added saving high scores under a name in Tetramental, I had to keep the calls to the site out of the [itch.io](http://itch.io) build. That copy is just files, no server, so those requests would fail. I kept that code out of the standalone build, then rebuilt it and searched the packaged files for calls to the site. It took the better part of a day iterating to get it right, and I manually reviewed it to make sure there's nothing that pointed back to the site. Then implemented a guard in the packager that stops with an error if there are any site references.

Testing tools: The arena is works in a different way and uses other tools. It plays a version of a computer player against the player using the game's own engine, with the same game seed. I built and used a test harness runnable by Haiku agents to tune arena matches and exams. On the Endless Path (a progressively harder mode), there's similar functionality, but it doesn't measure the new two-opponent exams that keep getting harder with no ceiling. It's up to the player to find out just how difficult they get -- I don't expect anyone to beat them in the current state of the game, but you never know. Later there will be additional, more powerful abilities that make those more possible. At that point, I'll adjust the test tools to cover it.
